text: A trained TinyGPT doesn't output words — at every step it outputs logits, one raw score per vocabulary token. Turning those scores into an actual chosen token is a separate decision, and that choice alone can make the same model sound robotic or lively. This lesson covers the four sampling strategies you'll actually reach for.

You only care about the logits at the final position, shape batch by vocab size, since that's the prediction for whatever comes next. Greedy decoding just takes the argmax of that row every time — fully deterministic, same prompt always gives the same output, but it never considers a close second-best, which tends to produce flat, repetitive text.

Temperature divides the logits before the softmax. Below one, it sharpens the distribution and behaves more like greedy. Above one, it flattens things out, giving lower-probability tokens a real shot and producing more varied, occasionally less coherent text. Temperature alone doesn't remove any tokens from consideration — it just reshapes the odds.

Top-k sampling actually narrows the candidate pool: torch dot topk grabs the k highest-scoring tokens, you renormalize just those into a distribution, and torch dot multinomial draws one at random according to those weights. That's the real randomness in sampling, as opposed to argmax's deterministic pick — and cutting the long tail first means you never randomly land on an implausible token.

Top-k always keeps a fixed count, but the right number of plausible tokens actually changes step to step. Top-p, or nucleus sampling, keeps a variable-size set instead — the smallest group of tokens whose cumulative probability crosses p. When the model's confident, the nucleus shrinks to almost nothing; when it's uncertain, it grows. That adaptiveness is why top-p is the default in most modern generation libraries.

Greedy for reproducibility, top-k or top-p with a bit of temperature for text that actually reads as natural — there's no universally right answer, only the right tool for what you're generating. Up next, lesson forty-three: now that you can generate text, how do you measure whether it's actually any good?
